analysis.one_liner: Bans PFAS 'forever chemicals' from food packaging like wrappers and takeout containers.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban PFAS in food containers never got a committee vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made 'forever chemicals' used to grease-proof fast-food wrappers, takeout boxes, and other food packaging, and they can migrate into the food people eat; they don't break down in the body or the environment. The bill would change federal food-safety law so that, starting January 1, 2022, any PFAS chemical used in materials that touch food would be deemed unsafe and the packaged food treated as adulterated — an effective national ban. Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced it in May 2019, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, where it stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who eats food sold or served in packaging — especially fast-food and takeout customers, including children, who studies have shown ingest small amounts of PFAS from grease-resistant wrappers and containers. Reducing exposure lowers the long-term risks tied to PFAS, which have been linked in scientific and regulatory reviews to health problems such as cancer, liver and thyroid effects, immune suppression, and elevated cholesterol, and which persist in the body for years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who eats packaged or takeout food

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act so that any PFAS used as a food contact substance is 'deemed unsafe' beginning January 1, 2022, making food packaged with it legally adulterated [S3].

A food contact substance is any material used in manufacturing, packing, packaging, transporting, or holding food, so the ban covers wrappers, containers, and other packaging that touches what people eat [S2].
PFAS are defined broadly — any man-made chemical with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom — which prevents companies from simply swapping to a close chemical cousin to dodge the ban [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical companies that make PFAS-based grease-proofing agents and the food-packaging and restaurant chains that buy them would have to reformulate products before the January 2022 deadline, replacing PFAS coatings with alternatives such as wax or non-fluorinated barriers. Those costs could show up modestly in packaging prices, though several large restaurant and grocery chains had already begun phasing out PFAS packaging on their own.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on chemical and packaging suppliers and downstream on restaurant and grocery businesses, which would need to reformulate grease-proof coatings on a fixed federal deadline [S3].

The bill bans the entire PFAS class in food packaging by default with no safety-by-use assessment, so some compounds that regulators might have cleared for limited use with low migration would be prohibited anyway; an honest supporter acknowledges this blunt approach trades precision for speed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: PFAS are persistent chemicals that build up in the body, and food packaging is a recognized exposure route, so removing them from wrappers and containers directly reduces what people ingest. The main cost is transition expense for a handful of packaging suppliers, several of whom were already moving away from PFAS amid consumer and retailer pressure. The main design weakness is that the class-wide ban is blunt rather than risk-calibrated, but for a chemical class defined by its persistence, that bluntness is arguably the point. On balance the benefits to public health outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in May 2019 and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the Keep Food Containers Safe from PFAS Act on May 17, 2019 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and three days later to its Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action — no subcommittee vote, no committee markup, no floor vote — is recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
The bill drew only one cosponsor in two and a half years, so it never built the coalition that forces committee action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and food-packaging suppliers kept selling grease-proofing chemicals for food contact through the entire 116th Congress, with no federal ban ever put to a vote. Consumers kept eating food packaged with PFAS; the same class-wide approach passed state-level bans elsewhere, but no federal version became law in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS and packaging makers; the ban died quietly

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.role: U.S. Representative, Michigan's 12th District; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban PFAS in food contact substances and referred it to committee.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee and its Health Subcommittee held the bill for the rest of the Congress without a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no record shows how parties would have split; the bill had a Democratic sponsor, one Democratic cosponsor, and died in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill deems every PFAS in food packaging unsafe from January 2022, eliminating the market for grease-proofing agents in food contact materials. Their interest in keeping those products legal runs directly against reducing public exposure to persistent chemicals in food.

Suppliers would have had to reformulate grease-resistant coatings before the deadline. Their interest in cheaper, unchanged packaging runs against the public's interest in lower PFAS intake, though some had already begun phasing PFAS out.

The mandate would have raised packaging compliance costs, but it also leveled the field for chains that had voluntarily quit PFAS packaging and shielded them from consumer concern about 'forever chemicals' in their wrappers.
